title: Solidity — Arrays, Structs, Mappings & Storage vs Memory
author: Blockchain Lectures

slides.title: Arrays, Structs & Mappings
slides.subtitle: Lecture #3 — How Real Applications Store Data in Solidity
slides.tagline: Master these three data structures and you can build Student Systems, DeFi protocols, NFT projects and DAOs

slides.title: Revision — What We Learned in Lecture 2
slides.definition: In Lecture 2 we learned the complete foundation of Solidity programming. Today we build directly on top of that foundation to store and manage collections of real-world data.
keyPoints: Data types: uint, int, bool, string, address — every variable has an explicit type in Solidity
State variables vs local variables — state persists on blockchain; local exists only during function call
Storage (permanent, costly) vs Memory (temporary, cheap) vs Calldata (read-only, cheapest)
Functions: visibility (public, private, internal, external), view (reads state), pure (no state access)
Constructor: runs once at deployment; msg.sender = the deployer address; used to set contract owner
So far we stored SINGLE values only — string public name; uint public age — today we store COLLECTIONS

slides.title: Why We Need Data Structures
slides.definition: Until now we stored one value at a time. Real applications need to store hundreds or thousands of records — students, employees, products, voters, users. Declaring individual variables for each record is impossible. Solidity solves this with three powerful data structures.
keyPoints: Problem: storing 500 students with uint mark1; uint mark2; ... uint mark500; is completely impractical
Arrays — store multiple values of the SAME type in order: marks of all students, list of all addresses
Structs — group DIFFERENT types under one name: a Student has a name (string), age (uint), department (string)
Mappings — link a KEY to a VALUE like a lookup table: address → balance, address → user profile
These three structures are the backbone of EVERY real Solidity contract — ERC-20 tokens use mappings for balances, NFT contracts use arrays for token lists, DAOs use mappings for voter records
By the end of today you will build a complete Student Management System using all three

slides.title: Arrays — Storing Multiple Values of the Same Type
slides.subtitle: Topic 1 — Arrays
slides.explanation: An array is a collection of multiple values of the same data type stored in sequence. Each value occupies a numbered position called an index, starting at 0. Instead of declaring four separate variables for four marks, you declare one array.
slides.note: Index always starts at 0 — first element is marks[0], second is marks[1], and so on

slides.title: Arrays — Complete Code Example
slides.subtitle: Deploy this in Remix and test step by step

codeBlocks.label: Full Contract

keyPoints: uint[] public numbers — declares a dynamic array of unsigned integers; starts empty []
numbers.push(_number) — appends the new value to the END of the array; array grows by 1
numbers.length — built-in property; returns current count of elements as uint
numbers.pop() — removes and deletes the LAST element; array shrinks by 1; cannot pop from empty array
numbers(0) in Remix — the public keyword auto-generates a getter that accepts an index
Fixed-size array syntax: uint[5] public fixed — size is locked at compile time; no push or pop allowed

slides.title: Structs — Grouping Related Data Together
slides.subtitle: Topic 2 — Structs
slides.explanation: A struct is a custom data type that groups multiple different types under one name. Think of it like a row in a database table — each column can be a different type. Arrays store one type; structs group many types for one record.
slides.problem: Problem — an array cannot store different types together:
slides.problemCode:
// WRONG — cannot mix types in one array
// name? age? department? — three different types
slides.solution: Solution — a struct holds all fields in one record:
slides.note: A struct is like a template — you define it once and then create as many Student instances as you need

slides.title: Structs — Complete Code Example
slides.subtitle: A single student record with getter and setter

codeBlocks.label: Full Contract

keyPoints: struct Student { } — defines the template; this does NOT create any variable or use storage yet
Student public student — NOW we declare one actual Student variable in contract storage
student = Student(_name, _age, _department) — creates a new Student instance and stores it
student.name — dot notation accesses individual fields of the struct
string memory — reference types in function parameters MUST declare memory or calldata location
The public auto-getter for a struct returns ALL fields at once as a tuple in Remix
practicalSteps: Click the student button → see all three fields returned
Call setStudent('Sara', 22, 'AI') to overwrite — only one record is stored

slides.title: Struct Arrays — Storing Multiple Records
slides.subtitle: Combining structs + arrays to store a list of students

codeBlocks.label: Full Contract

keyPoints: Student[] public students — an array where EACH element is a full Student struct (not just a uint)
students.push(Student(_name, _age)) — creates a Student struct inline and appends it to the array
students.length — works identically on struct arrays; returns total number of Student records
Student memory s = students[_index] — copies one struct from storage into memory for reading; cheaper than multiple storage reads
Returns a tuple (string memory, uint) — Solidity supports multiple return values natively
This pattern is the foundation of NFT ownership lists, employee registries, product catalogs

slides.title: Mappings — The Most Important Data Structure
slides.subtitle: Topic 3 — Mappings (spend time here)
slides.explanation: A mapping is a key-value store — like a lookup table or a dictionary. You give it a key, it instantly returns the associated value. Think of a bank: given an account number (key), it returns the balance (value). In Ethereum, the key is almost always an address.
slides.syntaxNote: address is the KEY type — uint is the VALUE type — any types can be used

slides.title: Mappings — Complete Code Example
slides.subtitle: Store and retrieve balances per wallet address

codeBlocks.label: Full Contract

keyPoints: mapping(address => uint) — the KEY is an address, the VALUE is a uint; declared in storage automatically
balances[msg.sender] = _amount — writes to the mapping; msg.sender is the wallet calling this function
balances[_addr] — reads from the mapping; reading an address that never set a balance returns 0 (default) — no error
balances[msg.sender] += _amount — read-then-write in one line; increments existing value
Mappings CANNOT be iterated — you cannot loop over all keys; you must know the key to access the value
Mappings CANNOT be passed as function arguments or returned from functions — storage only
practicalSteps: Deploy with Wallet A — call setBalance(100)
Switch to Wallet B in Remix — call setBalance(500)
Switch back to Wallet A — call getBalance(WalletA address) → 100
Query a random address → returns 0 (not an error)

slides.title: Mapping + Struct — Real-World Pattern
slides.subtitle: Every wallet stores its own full profile — the most common DeFi pattern

codeBlocks.label: Full Contract

keyPoints: mapping(address => User) — the value is a full struct, not just a uint; each address owns a unique profile
users[msg.sender] = User(_name, _age, true) — creates a User struct inline and stores it at msg.sender's slot
!users[msg.sender].registered — dot notation works on mapped structs; checks the bool field
require(!users[msg.sender].registered, 'Already registered') — prevents duplicate registration
This exact pattern is used in: ERC-20 token balances (mapping(address=>uint)), NFT ownership (mapping(uint=>address)), DeFi staking (mapping(address=>StakeInfo struct))
users[_addr].name — you can access individual struct fields directly through the mapping
practicalSteps: Deploy — call register('Ali', 20) with Wallet A
Call register('Ali', 20) again with same wallet → REVERTS: 'Already registered'
Switch to Wallet B — call register('Sara', 22) — each wallet has its own profile

slides.title: Storage vs Memory — Where Does Data Live?
leftItems: Lives permanently on the blockchain — survives after the function ends, after the transaction, forever
All state variables (declared outside functions) are automatically in storage
SSTORE opcode: writing to storage costs 20,000 gas for a new slot, 5,000 gas to update — the most expensive EVM operation
SLOAD opcode: reading storage costs 2,100 gas (cold access) or 100 gas (warm access, EIP-2929)
Example: Student[] public students — the array and all its elements live in storage permanently
Example: mapping(address => uint) public balances — every balance stored forever on-chain
Gas tip: minimize storage writes; batch updates; use events for data that does not need on-chain queries
rightItems: Lives only during the execution of ONE function call — completely erased when the function returns
Required keyword for reference types (string, bytes, arrays, structs) in function parameters and local variables
Cost: ~3 gas per byte — roughly 100x cheaper than storage for the same data
Example: string memory _name — the string lives in memory during the function; not stored unless you write it to a state variable
Example: Student memory s = students[0] — copies struct from storage to memory for cheap local access
Cannot return memory variables from external calls that persist — memory is per-call only
Rule: if data only needs to exist during computation, use memory; if it must persist, write it to a storage state variable

slides.title: Practical Project — Student Management System
slides.subtitle: The complete contract combining Arrays + Structs + Mappings

codeBlocks.label: Full Contract

keyPoints: struct Student — custom type grouping name, age, department (three different types)
Student[] public students — array of structs; stores every student permanently on-chain
mapping(address => bool) hasRegistered — prevents one wallet from registering multiple times
require(!hasRegistered[msg.sender]) — guard check at the top of addStudent; reverts if already registered
students.push(Student(_name, _age, _department)) — creates and appends a new Student in one line
require(_index < students.length) — prevents array out-of-bounds access; always validate index
Student memory s = students[_index] — copies to memory first; more gas-efficient for multiple field reads
practicalSteps: Try addStudent again with Wallet A → REVERTS: 'You already registered a student'

slides.title: Real-World Connections — Why This Matters
leftItems: ERC-20 Token Contract — uses mapping(address => uint256) balances to store every holder's token balance; mapping(address => mapping(address => uint256)) allowances for approvals
NFT (ERC-721) Contract — uses mapping(uint256 => address) ownerOf to store who owns each token ID; mapping(address => uint256) balanceOf for count
DeFi Staking Protocol — uses mapping(address => StakeInfo) stakes where StakeInfo is a struct with { uint amount; uint timestamp; uint rewards }
DAO Voting System — uses mapping(address => bool) hasVoted to prevent double voting; struct Proposal { string title; uint yesVotes; uint noVotes; bool executed }
Marketplace Contract — uses Listing[] public listings (struct array) to display all active listings; mapping(uint => address) seller to track who listed each item
rightItems: Student Management System — struct for student record + array to list all students + mapping to prevent duplicates
Simple Token — mapping(address => uint) balances + transfer function + events (next lecture)
Voting Contract — struct Candidate with name + voteCount + array of all candidates + mapping to prevent double voting
Product Registry — struct Product with name, price, stock + array for listing + mapping(address => Product[]) for per-seller products
Todo List — struct Task with title + bool completed + array of tasks + owner-only access via msg.sender
User Profile System — mapping(address => User) where User struct has name, age, bio + register() + update() functions

slides.title: Lecture #3 Summary — Key Takeaways
points: Arrays store multiple values of the same type in order — uint[] uses push() to add, pop() to remove last, .length for count
Structs define a custom data type grouping different types under one name — like a database row with named columns
Struct Arrays combine both: Student[] stores hundreds of full Student records permanently on-chain
Mappings are key-value stores — mapping(address => uint) gives instant O(1) lookup; unset keys return default value (0, false, address(0)) — never an error
Mapping + Struct is the most powerful real-world pattern — every DeFi protocol, NFT project, and DAO uses it
Storage is permanent and expensive (20,000 gas per new slot); Memory is temporary and cheap (3 gas/byte) — always declare memory for reference type function parameters
You can now build: Student Management System, simple Token, Voting Contract, User Registry — all the foundational dApp patterns
slides.closing: Arrays, Structs, and Mappings are the foundation of every real Solidity contract — from ERC-20 tokens to DeFi protocols to NFTs.
